lesson.title: Thou -st Drill Circuit
lesson.subtitle: du -st across five verbs — Shakespeare as muscle memory

hook.title: The Circuit
hook.content: One ending, five verbs, no mercy: du lernst, du kommst, du trinkst, du machst, du denkst. The -st you attach is not German's invention — it is the exact ending of Early Modern English: thou learn'st, thou comest, thou drinkest. Shakespeare conjugated German before Germany standardized it. Run the circuit until adding -st feels as automatic as it felt to a 1600s English speaker — because historically, it is the same gesture.

footnotes.title: The Second/Third Pairing
footnotes.content: du -st and er -t ride together: lernst/lernt, kommst/kommt, denkst/denkt. In old English: thou learnest, he learneth. The consonants of the endings are identical; only the vowel spelling drifted apart.

pattern.title: Run the Circuit
pattern.content: lernen: du lernst, er lernt. kommen: du kommst, er kommt. trinken: du trinkst, er trinkt. machen: du machst, er macht. denken: du denkst, er denkt — and sein refuses the pattern, as always: du bist (thou art!), er ist. Notice the circuit never asks the stem to change: komm-, trink-, mach-, denk- stay solid while only the tail rotates. In sentences, du-verbs sit in position 2 like anyone else — and in questions the verb even leads: Kommst du morgen?
pattern.linguist_note: Kommst du? is verb-first inversion — the question form English rebuilt with do-support ('Do you come?'). German kept the older Germanic way: swap subject and verb, add nothing. Archaic English agrees: 'Knowest thou?'

exercises.explanation: du bist is the exact twin of 'thou art' — sein kept one of the oldest forms in either language.

exercises.explanation: du + denkst in position 2, and the accusative mich closes the thought — 'thou thinkest of me'.

summary.outcome: Conjugate five verbs in du and er forms on sight, including the sein exception.

use_example.english: You think of me (thou thinkest of me).

summary.takeaway: du -st / er -t across every regular verb — the Shakespearean circuit — with du bist as the lone rebel.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: pronouns as case anchors — the him-case: why der becomes den and English him proves it.

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

denken.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Shares the exact vowel-shift relationship with "danken" that English has in "think" and "thank" (a thank is a good thought).

du.etymology_derivation: Direct cognate of archaic English "thou". Conjugates with -st (thou goest ↔ du gehst).

mädchen.context_translation: The girl is reading a book.
mädchen.etymology_derivation: Magd (maid) + diminutive -chen; Magd and English maid share Proto-Germanic *magadiz. -chen is always neuter. [wiktionary]

nase.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nasō — English nose comes from an alternative Germanic form. [wiktionary]

bahnhof.etymology_derivation: Bahn (track) + Hof (yard) — the track-yard; a transparent compound of German parts. [wiktionary]

rechnen.etymology_derivation: The twin of English reckon — the entry lists English reckon as its English cognate, both from the PIE root *h₃reǵ-. [wiktionary]

hageln.etymology_derivation: Weak verb from Hagel (hail); the page compares Dutch hagelen and English hail (verb) directly — German weather verbs work like it rains: es regnet, es schneit, es hagelt. [wiktionary]

echt.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German echt 'lawful, genuine', from ē 'law' — related to German Ehe 'marriage', the lawful bond; English uses echt as a loan from German. [wiktionary]

schein.context_translation: He pays with a ten-euro note.
schein.etymology_derivation: From the scheinen (shine) family — the page lists English shine as cognate; a banknote is literally a shine, what glints in the hand. [wiktionary]

feuerwehr.context_translation: The fire brigade puts out the fire.
feuerwehr.etymology_derivation: Feuer (fire, a documented twin) plus Wehr (defense) from the ward-off root *warjaną; the related Wehr entry names English weir — a river weir is a Wehr in the water. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
